legendEntries.label: A gate: the whole agreement passes through it before the work starts
Back up a layer when something is not working

nodes.label: Before anything is written
nodes.note: Nothing is decided yet. People notice something they share and find each other.

nodes.label: What we all take for granted
nodes.note:
The unwritten layer: what feels fair, who counts, what the group is for. Writing it down as a preamble makes it something people can point at and argue with.

Ostrom's word: metaconstitutional.

nodes.label: Deciding who sets the rules
nodes.note:
Who is in, what seats exist, how the group decides, how these rules can change, and who watches the whole thing ethically.

Ostrom's word: constitutional.

nodes.label: Setting the house rules
nodes.note:
The everyday rules, made and changed by the group: taking and giving, keeping an eye out, what happens first and then, where arguments go.

Ostrom's word: collective choice.

nodes.label: Doing the work
nodes.note:
Living by the rules, and watching how things really work.

Ostrom's word: operational.

nodes.label: Two examples all the way through: the Elm Street garden, and the RCN Constitution (written with the Constitution Builder)
Name what we share
nodes.note:
1. What is the shared thing, what do people take from it, who uses it, and what goes wrong?

Elm Street: one rain-fed tank, 30 plots, and not enough water in August.
RCN: know-how and tools for neighborhoods (open to all, so the trouble is getting people to contribute), plus time and server costs that Marc carries.

nodes.label: Gather the founders
nodes.note:
2. Who is at the first table? Before any rule exists, this decides whose voice shapes all the others. Ask who is missing.

Elm Street: the neighbors who asked the city for the lot.
RCN: self-declared, 'at present we are seven' (Article II), in groups of 5 to 15.

nodes.label: Say what we take for granted
nodes.note:
3. What do we believe is fair? What are we for? Write the unwritten down, so it can be pointed at and argued with.

Elm Street: everyone who wants to grow food should be able to.
RCN: the Preamble's seven beliefs (the primacy of the local, working together, ...) and 'fairness is our superordinate condition for action'.

nodes.label: Write the founding rules
nodes.note:
4. Who is in? What seats are there? How do we decide? How can these rules change? Who outside has to recognize us?

Elm Street: members are plot holders; the spring meeting decides by two-thirds; the city lease.
RCN: one class of member, every voice equal (III §1); amended by consensus, reviewed yearly (V §3); an unincorporated network (II §1).

nodes.label: Build in the ethical check
nodes.note:
5. Who watches the whole thing for fairness, with real power to warn and to stop? Ethics beyond the personal needs standing, and only founding rules can give it.

Elm Street: a few gardeners speak each season for the watershed, the neighbors, and the newcomers on the waiting list.
RCN: the Preamble's ethical regulation and the Ethical Oversight Framework: seven points of view, warnings first, vetoes when needed.

nodes.label: Start the house rules small
nodes.note:
6. Write only the house rules you need now. Add the rest as real problems show up, each one checked as it goes in.

Elm Street: watering days; the keeper; a word first, then a week without water.
RCN: Article III §2 to §5 and Article IV: share innovations, lightweight facilitation on Thursdays, 'our operating norms are largely implicit'.

nodes.label: Check every sentence
nodes.note:
7. A gate. Gaps go back to whichever step wrote the sentence. Run every sentence through the Agreement Checker. Look for things nobody created, rules with no 'or else', and triggers nobody reads. Then read the profile of what long-lasting groups do.

Elm Street: who reads the tank?
RCN: a first reading finds 'Decisions are made ad hoc' (III §3), no stated way of deciding, and mostly expectations rather than rules.

nodes.label: Agree to it together
nodes.note:
8. A gate. Everyone at the founding table agrees, and the record says how they agreed. The founding agreement can't be made by a vote, because no voting rule exists yet.

Elm Street: everyone at the first meeting says yes, and their names are written down.
RCN: the Ratification line on the Constitution page still has a blank date and no signatures.

nodes.label: Live it, watch it, change it
nodes.note:
9. Do the work. Keep track of how things really work against what was written. Take problems up to the layer that can fix them.

Elm Street: a tank chart by the gate; the spring meeting changes what is not working.
RCN: weekly Thursday calls, yearly review (V §3), the eVSM for the health of the whole (V §2), and the ethical check's regular convergence.

nodes.label: Seven points of view
nodes.note:
The ethical check, made operational in the RCN Ethical Oversight Framework, after Mick Ashby's Ethical Regulator Theorem.

Future Generations, Adjacent Communities, The Living Environment, The Marginalized Insider, The Informed Outsider, The Historical Record, The Systemic View.

About five people per point of view, each person in at least two, so the whole stays visible in each part. Outputs: warnings (the system working), vetoes (rare, real), and dated assessments, all posted publicly on FedWiki.

edges.label: creates
edges.note: The founding rules create the ethical check and give it standing to halt action.

edges.label: warning, then veto
edges.note: Warnings come before a line is crossed; a veto stops action and says what would lift it.

edges.label: a house rule is not working
edges.note: Most problems are fixed one layer up, by the group changing a house rule.

edges.label: the problem keeps coming back
edges.note: A rule problem that keeps coming back is usually a founding-rule problem: someone without a seat, or no agreed way of deciding.

story.text: Founding moves down the layers of deciding. First people notice what they share and find each other. Then they say what they take for granted, write the founding rules, and build in an ethical check. Then they write the house rules, small. Everything passes two gates, a check of every sentence and an agreement by everyone at the table, before the work begins. Once the work is going, the dashed arrows climb back up whenever something isn't working.
## The nine steps

1. [[Name What We Share]]
2. [[Gather The Founders]]
3. [[Say What We Take For Granted]]
4. [[Write The Founding Rules]]
5. [[Build In The Ethical Check]], which creates [[Seven Points Of View]]
6. [[Start The House Rules Small]]
7. [[Check Every Sentence]]
8. [[Agree To It Together]]
9. [[Live It Watch It Change It]]
## Two examples all the way through
The Elm Street garden is imagined: 30 plots, one rain-fed water tank, a water keeper, a spring meeting, land leased from the city. It keeps every step concrete.

The RCN Constitution is real. It was written with the [Constitution Builder](https://ndcgroup.relocalizecreativity.net/constitution-builder.html), which organizes a constitution by Donella Meadows' leverage points, and it carries an ethical safeguard taken from Mick Ashby's Ethical Regulator Theorem, made operational in the RCN Ethical Oversight Framework. The framework says it will be worked out in RCN first and then applied to NDC constitutions. Each step page shows what the RCN Constitution already does at that step, and what an NDC would still have to decide.
## Two lessons that shape the path

Start small. Ostrom found that rules that work grow piece by piece, fitted to their place. A complete set of rules written in one sitting is mostly rules on paper. So the path writes only three things at the start, who's in, how we decide, and how we change these rules, and grows the house rules as real problems show up.

Mind the founding puzzle. You can't vote on how to vote. The first rules can only be agreed by everyone at the first table, which makes who sits at that table the most important decision of all. That is why gathering the founders comes before any rule is written.
## Where the other tools fit

The Constitution Builder writes the content of steps 3 to 6. The Ethical Oversight Framework is step 5. The Agreement Checker is step 7. The decks "Governing What We Share" explain the vocabulary, one layer at a time. SPC charts, the protection survey and the Relationship Record serve step 9.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

item.text: *Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: Step 1. Before anyone writes a rule, say plainly what is shared and what goes wrong with it.
## The plain questions

- What is the shared thing? What do people take from it or put into it?
- Does it run out when people use it? Can we keep people out?
- Who uses it now, and who is affected but doesn't use it?
- What goes wrong today, and when?
## What gets written

A short description everyone can agree is true, before anyone argues about what to do. The answers to the two questions (does it run out, can we keep people out) tell you the kind of trouble to expect: things taken too fast, or nobody pitching in.
## At Elm Street

One rain-fed tank, 30 plots, and in August not enough water for everyone. The water runs out, and it's hard to stop people watering, so the trouble is both taking too much and not putting back. Neighbors without plots are affected too: the garden is on their street.
## In the RCN Constitution

What RCN shares is mostly know-how and tools for neighborhoods, given away freely (Article II §1, Article IV §2: everything produced is open). Know-how doesn't run out and nobody is kept out, so the trouble is the other kind: getting enough people to contribute. RCN also shares something that does run out: time, attention, and the cost of the Zoom and FedWiki servers, which the Constitution says Marc covers (Article IV §2).
For an NDC: what does the neighborhood share? Land, a fund, a building, care, food? Each answer brings a different kind of trouble.
## Ostrom's words

The shared thing and the bits taken from it: resource system and resource units. Does it run out: subtractability. Can we keep people out: excludability. Something that runs out and is hard to fence off: a common-pool resource.
Next: [[Gather The Founders]]. Back to [[Founding A Commons Step By Step]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: Step 2. Who sits at the first table? Before any rule exists, this decides whose voice shapes all the others.
## The plain questions

- Who is here now, and why?
- Who uses the shared thing but isn't here? Who is affected but isn't here?
- Who has the least voice, and how will they get to the table?
- How many of us is right to start? Enough to do the work, few enough to know each other.
## Why this comes first

You can't vote on how to vote. The first rules can only be agreed by everyone at the founding table, so whoever is missing from that table is missing from every rule that follows. A seat left out now is the hardest kind to add later.
## What gets written
A list of founders, and a plain note of who was invited and couldn't come, and who is still missing.
## At Elm Street
The neighbors who asked the city for the lot. Missing at first: the renters on the next block who would garden if they knew, and the family across the street whose kids play there.
## In the RCN Constitution

RCN is self-declared: "an unincorporated network of local activists" where each member and neighborhood decides for itself (Article II §1). "At present we are seven," and groups of 5 to 15 work well (Article II §2).
For an NDC: who are the founders, and who speaks for the people with least voice from the very first meeting? This is where a community health worker's seat is won or lost.
## Ostrom's words
Who is at the founding table: the first boundary decision, made before any written boundary rule. The people with least voice: in the RCN Ethical Oversight Framework, The Marginalized Insider.
Next: [[Say What We Take For Granted]]. Back: [[Name What We Share]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

say-what-we-take-for-granted.title: Say What We Take For Granted

story.text: Step 3. Write down the unwritten: what feels fair, who counts, what this is for. Once it's written, people can point at it and argue with it.
## The plain questions

- What do we believe is fair?
- What are we for, and what will we never do?
- Who counts? Who do we owe something to who isn't here (the land, the neighbors, people not yet born)?
- How far ahead are we looking?
## What gets written
A preamble: a page of plain beliefs and a purpose. It isn't a rule; nothing in it can be enforced. But every rule written later can be checked against it.
## At Elm Street
"Everyone who wants to grow food here should be able to. The water belongs to the garden, not to whoever gets there first. We leave the soil better than we found it."
## In the RCN Constitution

The Preamble states seven beliefs: the primacy of the local; the necessity of working together; a view of human nature (diversity is strength, participation is the antidote to isolation and domination); our relationship to the environment; our time horizon; our system boundaries; our theories of change. Then the commitment that matters most for everything after: "Fairness is our superordinate condition for action. Nothing proceeds at any level without checking for fairness." The Constitution Builder files this under Meadows' leverage points 1 and 2, paradigm and the ability to transcend it.
For an NDC: what does this neighborhood take for granted, and is any of it unfair to someone who isn't at the table yet?
## Ostrom's words
What we all take for granted: the metaconstitutional level. It is the strongest layer because it is unwritten, which is why writing some of it down matters.
Next: [[Write The Founding Rules]]. Back: [[Gather The Founders]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: Step 4. The few rules that decide who sets all the other rules. Start with three, and add only what you need.
## The three rules to start with

- Who's in: who counts as a member, how you join, how you leave.
- How we decide: a vote, two-thirds, everyone agrees, one person. Say it out loud; most quarrels come from people assuming different ways of deciding.
- How we change these rules: who may propose, how it is decided, how often they are reviewed.
## Then, as needed

- What seats there are: roles, and how people come to hold them.
- Who outside has to recognize us: a lease, a legal form, a permit.
- What groups we belong to that are bigger than us.
## At Elm Street

Members are plot holders, and anyone on the waiting list may attend the meeting. The spring meeting decides by two-thirds of those present. These rules change only at the spring meeting, by the same two-thirds. The city leases the land year to year.
## In the RCN Constitution

Who's in: "All participation in the Network is voluntary. Every voice carries equal weight" (Article III §1), one class of member. How we change these rules: "a living document... reviewed annually and may be amended through consensus of active participants" (Article V §3). Who outside must recognize us: no one; RCN is an unincorporated network (Article II §1). How we decide everyday matters: "Decisions are made ad hoc" (Article III §3), which is the one founding rule the Constitution leaves open.

item.text: Step 4. The few rules that decide who sets all the other rules. Start with three, and add only what you need.
## The three rules to start with

- Who's in: who counts as a member, how you join, how you leave.
- How we decide: a vote, two-thirds, everyone agrees, one person. Say it out loud; most quarrels come from people assuming different ways of deciding.
- How we change these rules: who may propose, how it is decided, how often they are reviewed.
## Then, as needed

- What seats there are: roles, and how people come to hold them.
- Who outside has to recognize us: a lease, a legal form, a permit.
- What groups we belong to that are bigger than us.
## At Elm Street

Members are plot holders, and anyone on the waiting list may attend the meeting. The spring meeting decides by two-thirds of those present. These rules change only at the spring meeting, by the same two-thirds. The city leases the land year to year.
## In the RCN Constitution

Who's in: "All participation in the Network is voluntary. Every voice carries equal weight" (Article III §1), one class of member. How we change these rules: "a living document... reviewed annually and may be amended through consensus of active participants" (Article V §3). Who outside must recognize us: no one; RCN is an unincorporated network (Article II §1). How we decide everyday matters: "Decisions are made ad hoc" (Article III §3), which is the one founding rule the Constitution leaves open.
Also open, and noted on the RCN constitutional-arena drawing: who may teach, and what classes of member an NDC has. The Constitution governs RCN, not the enterprises it helps form.
## Ostrom's words

The founding rules: constitutional rules. Who's in: boundary rules. How we decide: aggregation rules. What seats: position rules. Outsiders recognizing us: recognition of rights (design principle 7). Groups within groups: nested enterprises (principle 8).
Next: [[Build In The Ethical Check]]. Back: [[Say What We Take For Granted]].

story.text: Step 5. Give someone the standing to warn, and if needed to stop, when the group drifts toward harm. Only the founding rules can give that standing.
## Why it belongs in the founding rules

Mick Ashby's Ethical Regulator Theorem says every organization that pursues goals needs a watcher above it, with enough ways of seeing to notice ethical drift, and the authority to step in before harm is done. Personal ethics needs no permission: I can decline to act. Ethics beyond the personal means stopping somebody else, and that is standing only founding rules can grant. A watcher created by the house rules can be overruled by the house rules.
## The plain questions

- Who watches, from which points of view?
- What can they do: warn, stop, require an answer?
- How are warnings answered, and in what time?
- Who watches the watchers? (The members, by changing the founding rules.)
## At Elm Street

Once a season, a few gardeners each speak for someone not at the meeting: the watershed downstream, the neighbors on the next block, the newcomers on the waiting list, the children who will garden here later. They can warn the meeting, and they can stop a decision until it has answered them.
## In the RCN Constitution

The Preamble's Ethical Regulation section requires a superordinate ethical metasystem with authority over management, the variety to see drift, independence, the power to halt, redirect or constrain, and accountability. The RCN Ethical Oversight Framework makes it operational as [[Seven Points Of View]]. Warnings come first; vetoes are rare and real; everything is posted publicly. The framework says it will be worked out in RCN and then applied to NDC constitutions.
## Ostrom's words
Ostrom has no direct term for this; it sits at the constitutional level, as a seat with standing over every arena below. Ashby's terms: ethical regulator, requisite variety.
Next: [[Start The House Rules Small]]. Back: [[Write The Founding Rules]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: The ethical check in practice, from the RCN Ethical Oversight Framework, after Mick Ashby's Ethical Regulator Theorem. Seven standpoints from which the group's actions look different. Together they give the watcher enough ways of seeing.
## The seven

- Future Generations: what does this foreclose or open for people not yet born?
- Adjacent Communities: who is affected but not at the table?
- The Living Environment: is this place more or less alive because of what we are doing?
- The Marginalized Insider: who among us has the least voice, and whose needs are assumed rather than asked?
- The Informed Outsider: what can't we see about ourselves?
- The Historical Record: what has happened before when people did this?
- The Systemic View: what does this do to the whole?
## How it runs

About five people hold each point of view, at least three, and each person sits in at least two, so the whole stays visible in each part. Groups set their own rhythm and meet together at a regular convergence.

They produce three things. Warnings, before a line is crossed: the system working. Vetoes, when a line will be or has been crossed: rare, real, naming what would lift them. Assessments: dated, so they fade and must be renewed. All are written plainly, signed by the group rather than by individuals, and posted on FedWiki. Whoever a warning is about has two weeks to answer in writing; silence goes to the convergence.
## At Elm Street

Four points of view are enough to begin: the watershed (The Living Environment), the next block (Adjacent Communities), the waiting list (The Marginalized Insider), and the children who will garden later (Future Generations).
Source: [RCN Constitution Notes](https://ndcgroup.relocalizecreativity.net/rcn-constitution-notes.html). Created by [[Build In The Ethical Check]]. Back to [[Founding A Commons Step By Step]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: Step 6. Write only the everyday rules you need now. Add the rest when a real problem shows up, and check each one as it goes in.
## The everyday rules a group usually needs, in time

- Taking and giving: who may take what, and what each person puts back, in fair proportion.
- Keeping an eye out: on each other and on the shared thing, by people who answer to the group.
- A word first, then step up: small consequences first, bigger for repeats.
- Settling it close to home: a cheap, quick place to take an argument, including an argument about the rules.
- Who gets told what, and when.
## What gets written
A short page of house rules, each one sentence. Each new rule is added when a real problem calls for it, and says when it applies, who it's for, must or may or must not, what, and or else what.
## At Elm Street

Water on your assigned days. No sprinklers when the tank is below half; the keeper reads the tank every Monday and posts the level on the gate. Four work hours a season per plot. A word from the keeper first; a second time, a week without water. Arguments go to the keeper, then to the spring meeting.
## In the RCN Constitution

Article III §2 to §5 and Article IV: everyone shares innovations and challenges; lightweight facilitation in Thursday meetings, where everyone can be heard; communication by WhatsApp, Zoom and FedWiki. Article III §5 says it honestly: "Our operating norms are largely implicit." That fits a small network that mostly needs coordination. An NDC holding land or money will need more of these written down.
## Ostrom's words

House rules: collective-choice and operational rules. The list follows design principles 2B (proportional costs and benefits), 4A and 4B (monitoring), 5 (graduated sanctions) and 6 (conflict resolution), plus information rules.
Next: [[Check Every Sentence]]. Back: [[Build In The Ethical Check]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: Step 7, a gate. Put every sentence of the draft through the Agreement Checker before anyone signs. Gaps go back to whichever step wrote the sentence.
## What the check looks for

- Things nobody created. A rule about "gardeners" with nothing saying who counts as one. A rule about "the tank" with nothing saying which tank.
- Rules with no "or else". Without one, a sentence is a hope, and people will drift from it.
- Triggers nobody reads. "When the tank is below half" assumes someone reads the tank.
- Penalties nobody carries out. Who applies the "or else", and who do they answer to?
- The eight things long-lasting groups do: which are present, partial, missing, or can't be told from the text.
## At Elm Street
The first draft said "no sprinklers when the tank is below half" but gave nobody the job of reading the tank. The check sent it back to step 6, which added the keeper's Monday reading.
## In the RCN Constitution

A first reading, not yet a full run of the Checker. Who's in is answered, and so is how the founding rules change. How everyday decisions are made is not: "Decisions are made ad hoc" (Article III §3). Most of the house rules are expectations and habits rather than rules with an "or else", which the Constitution itself says (Article III §5). The ethical veto has its conditions spelled out in the Ethical Oversight Framework rather than in the Constitution. Running the Checker on the full text is the next step.
## Ostrom's words

The checker codes each sentence with the Institutional Grammar (ADICO and IG 2.0): attribute, deontic, aim, object, conditions, or else; and creating sentences (constitutive statements). The profile is by design principle.
Next: [[Agree To It Together]]. Back: [[Start The House Rules Small]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

story.text: Step 8, a gate. Everyone at the founding table agrees, and the record says how they agreed.
## Why everyone, this once

The founding agreement can't be made by a vote, because no voting rule exists until it is adopted. So the first adoption is by everyone at the table. After that, the group changes its rules the way the rules themselves say.
## What gets written

- The date.
- Who agreed, by name.
- How they agreed: everyone present said yes.
- Who was invited and absent, and how they can add their agreement later.
- The ethical check's first assessment, if it has one.
## At Elm Street
At the first meeting all fourteen founders say yes. Their names go on the page with the date. The two who couldn't come sign the following week.
## In the RCN Constitution

The Ratification section reads "Date: _________ Signatures: _________". The Constitution has not yet recorded its own adoption. Filling in that line, and saying how it was agreed, is a small act that turns a draft into the network's founding rules.
For an NDC: plan the adoption meeting so the people with least voice are present, not just informed.
## Ostrom's words
The founding act happens at the constitutional level, made in the unwritten way the metaconstitutional level allows, because no written way of deciding exists yet.
Next: [[Live It Watch It Change It]]. Back: [[Check Every Sentence]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*

live-it-watch-it-change-it.title: Live It Watch It Change It

story.text: Step 9. Do the work, keep track of how things really work, and take problems up to the layer that can fix them.
## Three habits

- Watch: keep simple records over time of the shared thing and of who did what, kept with people, not about them.
- Compare: how things really work against what was written. A rule nobody follows has gone stale; a habit everybody follows is a rule nobody wrote down.
- Take it up a layer: a house rule that isn't working goes to the group (step 6); a problem that keeps coming back goes to the founding rules (step 4).
## At Elm Street

A chart of the tank level hangs on the gate, read every Monday. In the second August the keeper notices the same three plots run dry every week; the spring meeting changes the watering days. In the third year the waiting list has no voice at the meeting at all; that goes to the founding rules, which add a seat for it.
## In the RCN Constitution

Weekly Thursday calls and daily check-ins between Kerry and Marc (Article IV §3); goals reviewed with the same tools RCN builds for neighborhoods (Article I §4); the eVSM to assess the health of each organization and the whole network (Article V §2); a yearly review of the Constitution itself (Article V §3); and the regular convergence of the [[Seven Points Of View]].
## Ostrom's words
Doing the work: the operational level. How things really work: rules-in-use. Keeping track over time: monitoring (design principle 4), in RCN's case with SPC charts.
Back to [[Founding A Commons Step By Step]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026*
